It's actually not that hard.

First you GENTLY heat some cocoa butter in a bain marie. When it's molten you mix in some powdered sugar or dextrose or maybe some other source of sweet, then some cocoa powder and you've got basic molten chocolate. You can pour it out in anything you can pop it out of and let it cool down slowly until it goes solid.

I tend to use around 2:2:1 in cocoa butter, cocoa powder, sugar. So for example one ounce of cocoa butter, one ounce of cocoa powder and half an ounce of sugar. I have what people tell me are "dealer scales" to weigh small amounts so I'm not stuck with a huge block of chocolate I don't need right away.

If you put in less sugar, chocolate's bitterness starts to come out in force. If you like that, though, go for it. If you put in more cocoa powder, it becomes more dry and slightly more bitter, if you put in less it becomes a bit more fatty.

There's a LOT you could add, like nuts, spices, or pieces of dried fruit. You can vary what you use for sweetening, too. You could also use two ounces of entire cocoa beans and grind those if you have the equipment for it (I don't) since that's the source for cocoa powder and cocoa butter. They are usually separated in order to ensure you can control their dosage.

Milk chocolate you make with powdered milk substituting some part of the cocoa powder. Readily available powdered milk can leave your chocolate a bit grainy (but otherwise tasty) so decide for yourself if you're fanatical enough to grind your milk powder.

If you want white chocolate, just substitute the cocoa powder entirely. I almost always add some vanilla powder when adding any amount of milk powder, as well as ghee which allows me to more easily mix milk powder. A natural, dairy-based emulsifier is what it is.

You could also use different solid fats than cocoa powder, but I have never done that.

Most of the funky colored chocolate is just white chocolate with a coloring ingredient such as powdered green tea or strawberry sirup. A lot of people seem to like adding in cream or condensed milk to these, but that's not really my thing.

The absolutely fabulous part of all this is that anything which doesn't ruin the chocolate (be really sure everything has not one drop of water coming into contact with the chocolate while it's molten) could be added. You control what ingredient, what kind, and what form. If you want to know if X can be added, just make a small amount and add some X.

For any ingredient, keep in mind your main liquid is a type of fat which goes solid at room temperature. Things won't dissolve into it like with water. So if you want it to be spread equally throughout, it must be powdered or liquid in the bain marie. You're making a suspension, not a solution.

Above all else, though... keep notes. What did you do? How does the result taste? Be precise to ensure a consistent result.

What are the different types of mountain biking and what are their main differences?

Foreword: the following write-up is of my opinion and based on my experience with mountain biking. Also, as an owner of a Trek Remedy, I am a big fan of Trek, so all example bikes will be from Trek.

There are three main categories of mountain biking: cross country, enduro, and downhill, often referred to as gravity. Many may argue that there are subcategories or more categories that are grouped similar to enduro riding, such as trail and all-mountain. For sake of general discussion, I'm going to stick to cross country, enduro, and downhill.

The primary differences that set these different bike types are head and seat tube angles, amount of suspension travel, and wheel size. Cross country bikes are designed with aggressive angles to allow the rider to exert the maximum amount of force on the pedals to go as fast as they can at all times. Gravity bikes are much the opposite, with very slack geometries that allow the rider to more easily soak up big hits and jumps as gravity pulls them down the mountain. Enduro bikes balance the two, with geometry that sits somewhere in the middle so the rider can still achieve efficient pedalling for climbing while maintaining a somewhat slack head tube angle in order to handle the gnarly downhills.

Cross Country

Cross country bikes are all about speed. These bikes are commonly fit with fast-rolling 29" tires and light frames. Most World Cup racers still use hard tail bikes, but as suspension and frame design gets better, more and more full suspension bikes have been seen on the circuit. These bikes will have short suspension travel, often 100 mm, but there are plenty of offerings at 120 mm.

Contributing to their speed is their aggressive geometry. You will rarely find a cross country bike with a head tube angle of less than 70°. This keeps the rider in an upright and efficient position, allowing them to get all their power to the ground through the pedals.

See the Trek Top Fuel or Trek Procaliber.

Enduro

Often categorized alongside all-mountain and trail bikes, these bikes are designed for all-day adventure. These bikes will most likely be full suspension, with travel ranging from 130 mm to 160 mm. Wheel size will vary widely for enduro bikes, with most manufacturers offering 29" and 27.5"/650b options.

The slacker head tube angle, often between 66° and 69°, combined with the added suspension travel, will offer the rider smoother riding over the rough stuff. Many enduro bikes will also be outfitted with a dropper seatpost, to give the rider even more flexibility and control while descending.

See the Trek Remedy or Trek Slash.

Gravity

These bikes are purpose-built to go downhill, and go downhill fast. With most manufacturers offering 200 mm of travel in the front and back, there's not much out there that these can't handle. Wheel size has traditionally been 26" for gravity bikes, but many riders are starting to embrace 27.5"/650b wheels, and it looks like that trend will continue. The smaller wheel size allows the rider to really throw these bikes around while speeding downhill.

Head tube angles for gravity bikes are generally between 62° and 65°, which puts the front wheel plenty ahead of the rider. This keeps the rider from going over the handlebars when the going gets rough and at the same time provides great stability.

See the Trek Session.

In order to write very efficient code in C/C++ it is useful to understand how the C gets translated into machine code.

In a lot of cases your C/C++ code can work faster when you reorganize your C/C++ code to a point where it creates the most optimal assembly code.
for clarification... machine code is a form of VHDL? Because that's kind of how I see him explaining since that's what I had to do to program a 8086 chip instruction set...

VHDL is an FPGA programming language, while machine codes are instructions that directly use hardware-based instruction hard-coded in to a chip, called the instruction set. You can use VHDL or Verilog (basically same thing) to define the behavior of an FPGA to give it an instruction set, that you could then write machine code to program in.

I think it is way more important to know the compiler you're working with than to know the underlying assembly. You have to write code that the compiler will be able to optimize.

Then, read the assembly for critical part and make sure it was optimized correctly by the compiler.

Buy by analyzing the underlying assembly code can deduce how your compiler is creating the assembly language.
